video.title: Funeral In Every Religion Explained in 10 Minutes
video.description:
What happens when someone dies? In this video, we explore funeral traditions from different religions and cultures, including Christianity, Islam, Judaism, Hinduism, Buddhism, Zoroastrianism, and more.

From washing and wrapping the body, to cremation, burial, sky burials, and even the unusual rituals surrounding death, we look at what happens during a funeral and what each tradition believes happens after the body is laid to rest.

Based on religious texts, traditional teachings, and cultural practices, this video highlights both the similarities and the surprising differences between funeral traditions around the world.

transcript.text: Hinduism.
In Hinduism, funerals are usually very different from what we see in many Western religions.
In many Hindu traditions, the body is cremated, meaning it is placed on a funeral pyre and burned.
Before the cremation, the family washes and prepares the body.
In some traditions, a few drops of water from the Ganges are placed in the person's mouth.
Then they dress the body in fresh clothes and decorated with flowers.
The body gets carried to the cremation ground, usually before the next sunrise or sunset.
Traditionally, the eldest son has an important role.
He walks around the body while chanting.
In some traditions, he places rice in the mouth and pours ghee over the body and the wood.
Now, here's a detail most people don't know.
Before lighting the fire, they carry a pot of water around the body, then break it near the head.
Only after that do they light the fire.
Once the body starts burning, there's one more step.
Someone cracks open the skull with a stick.
It sounds intense, but the belief is that this releases the soul from the body completely.
A few days later, the family comes back, collects the ashes, and puts them in a sacred river, usually the Ganges.
This is the final step.
It means the soul is now fully free from the body.
Tibetan Buddhism.
One of the most unusual funeral traditions is called jhator.
It means giving alms to the birds, but most people know it as a sky burial.
After someone dies, monks and family members may pray for them.
Tibetan Buddhists believe the person enters a stage called Bardo.
This is the time between one life and the next.
It can last up to 49 days.
During this time, prayers are said for the person as they move toward their next life.
Instead of burying or burning the body, the body is taken to a special place in the mountains and offered to vultures.
Here's how it actually works.
A trained specialist called a rogyapa carries the body to a remote mountain top.
He burns incense to attract vultures, then using a ritual knife, he cuts the body into pieces, removing flesh from bone and feeding it directly to the birds.
After that, the bones get crushed and mixed with barley flower, making the mixture easier for the vultures to eat completely, so nothing gets left behind.
Family members usually aren't allowed to watch, and outsiders are strictly forbidden from observing or filming the ritual out of respect.
Tibetan Buddhists see the body as something temporary.
Once a person dies, the body is no longer needed, while their consciousness continues toward the next life.
Offering the body to animals is also seen as an act of generosity.
So instead of thinking of the body as something that must be preserved forever, Tibetan Buddhism focuses on what happens to the mind and consciousness after death.
Christianity.
Christian funerals are different depending on the church.
There's Catholic, Orthodox, and Protestant.
Each one treats the body a little differently.
Catholics usually have a viewing first, where people come to see the body one last time.
After that, there's a funeral mass led by a priest.
Burial has always been the traditional choice, because Catholics believe the body will one day be raised back to life.
But since 1963, the Catholic Church has also allowed cremation, as long as it's done respectfully and the ashes are buried instead of scattered or kept at home.
Orthodox Christians are stricter.
To them, cremation disrespects the body, since it's seen as sacred, meant to be reunited with the soul one day.
So burial is really the only option most Orthodox churches accept.
Before the funeral, there's often a vigil that can last up to three days, and the casket stays open so people can say a final goodbye.
And it doesn't stop there.
Orthodox families keep praying for the person eight days later, 40 days later, and again a year later.
Protestants are the most flexible of the three.
The Bible never says anything directly about cremation, so most Protestant churches just leave that choice up to the person or their family.
Protestant funerals are usually simpler, too.

transcript.text: from most other religions. Traditionally Zoroastrians do not bury or burn the body.
Instead the body is taken to a special structure called a Dokhma, often called a tower of silence.
But before that happens the body is washed and prayers are said.
A dog may also be brought near the body in a ritual called Sagdid.
The dog is believed to help drive away evil and protect the living from the pollution connected with death.
The body is then carried to the Dokhma.
It is a large open circular structure built away from the community.
The body is placed on the top where the sun wind and birds help break it down.
Over the next few days vultures eat the flesh leaving only the bones.
Over time the bones dry out and fall into the pit in the middle of the tower.
Why do they do this?
Zoroastrians consider fire, water, and earth sacred.
So traditionally a dead body is seen as impure.
So burying or burning it would contaminate something holy.
This tradition isn't as common today as it used to be. Here's why.
Farmers in India used to give a pain killer to sick livestock and other farm animals.
But that pain killer turned out to be deadly to vultures.
When vultures ate the bodies of animals that have been given the drug, the vultures died too.
Over time this wiped out most of the vulture population.
And since the whole tradition depends on vultures being there to consume the body, without enough vultures, the ritual just doesn't work anymore.
That's why a lot of Zoroastrian communities, especially in India, have had to switch to burial or cremation instead.
Islam. In Islam when a Muslim dies, the body is often buried within 24 hours.
First the body is washed in a ritual called Ghusl, usually done by family members of the same gender.
The body is carefully cleaned, and the washing is usually done three times.
The private parts of the body are kept covered, and the body is treated with respect throughout the process.
If it's a woman, her hair is washed and can be divided into three braids.
After the washing, the body is wrapped in a simple white cloth called a Kafan.
There are no fancy clothes.
The idea is that everyone is equal in death, whether they were rich or poor.
Then family, friends, and other Muslims gather for the funeral prayer called Salat al-Janazah.
Everyone stands while they pray for Allah to forgive the person and have mercy on them.
After that the body is carried to the grave and buried directly in the ground, on its right side facing Mecca.
After the burial the family is allowed to grieve and cry.
But Islam discourages crying too much or crying for too long.
For most relatives mourning should not continue beyond 3 days.
The main exception is a woman whose husband has died.
She observes a mourning period called Iddah, lasting 4 months and 10 days.
Toraja. In the Toraja culture of Indonesia, death does not always mean the person is immediately considered gone.
When someone dies, the family may keep the body in the house for weeks, months, or even years while they prepare for an elaborate funeral.
During this time the person may still be treated as if they are sick rather than dead.
The body is cleaned, dressed, and sometimes given food and drinks.
Torajan funerals are incredibly expensive.
Families have to save up sometimes for years to afford a proper ceremony which requires sacrificing water buffalo.
They believe the buffalo carries the soul into the afterlife to a place called Puya.
The more buffalo sacrificed, the higher someone's status in the next life.
When the family can finally afford the funeral, they hold a large ceremony called Rambu Solo.
It can last for several days, with relatives traveling from far away to attend.
Animals such as pigs and water buffalo may be sacrificed as part of the ceremony.
The more important the person was in the community, the larger the funeral may be.
After the ceremony the person is taken to a special burial place, often a cliff tomb carved into the rock.
Some families also place wooden statues called Tau Tau outside the tomb.
Every few years families hold a ritual called Manene.
They open the graves, pull out their relatives' bodies, clean them, comb their hair and dress them in fresh clothes.
